newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan battle resumes amid calls for peace.
newsitem.headline: Afghan battle resumes amid calls for peace.

text.p: Ousted government military commander Ahmad Shah Masood on Friday told Taleban fighters to quit Kabul, and backed his words with a hail of mortar and rocket fire north of the Afghan capital.

"We want the Taleban to evacuate Kabul," he told Reuters in the town of Jabal os-Siraj. "A limited international force under U.N. supervision should control Kabul and pave the way for all-party talks on a broad-based government."
Masood, who won renown as a guerrila leader for his exploits against occupying Soviet troops in the 1980s, made clear the alternative would be war.

As he spoke, mortar bombs and rockets from forces led by Masood rained down on positions around the key Bagram junction north of Kabul held by the purist Islamic Taleban militia, which drove him from the Afghan capital three weeks ago.
The Taleban replied with tank fire and multiple rocket launchers and huge clouds of brown dust soared into the grey sky on both sides of the front line.

But Taleban fighters near the front line just north of this market town a 45-minute drive north of Kabul said they had seen no signs of activity from the tanks and men sent in alongside Masood's by northern Uzbek chief Abdul Rashid Dostum.

Dostum sent a dozen tanks and several hundred men to join Masood on Thursday after formally recognising the government driven from Kabul and promising to back Masood if the Taleban did not stop fighting.
The Uzbeks held talks with Taleban leaders on Wednesday and Thursday, but there was no word on any outcome beyond a Taleban spokesman saying he was hopeful an understanding could be reached.
Masood reacted by calling on the Taleban for the second time in three days to quit Kabul.

"If the Taleban are not ready to cooperate with us, we cannot avoid fighting," Masood said in Jabal os-Siraj at the mouth of the Salang Pass through the Hindu Kush which his men retook in a counter-attack a week ago, he added.

A Taleban evacuation of Kabul was floated at the United Nations. The United States called it "probably premature", although State Department spokesman Nicholas Burms said a proposal to demilitarise Kabul was "an important idea".
There was no immediate reaction from the Taleban on Friday, the Islamic day of rest, but they rejected the earlier Masood ultimatum and vowed to defend Kabul.

Afghan watchers in Kabul say the static front line at Bagram Junction -- from which one road leads to the Salang and the other to the government's major airbase at Bagram and back to Kabul -- suggests Masood and the Taleban are evenly matched.
"Dostum will make all the difference, if he decides to fight," said one.

The Uzbek leader, who controls six of Afghanistan's 33 provinces from the northern city of Mazar-i-Sharif, has what is regarded as possibly the most potent fighting force in the country and a small air force.

"Deployment and talks are not necessarily inconsistent. Dostum is clearly making himself the key to a deal and his deployment just strengthens the pressure on the Taleban," said one veteran Afghan watcher.
Overnight reports of moves at the United Nations to find a way to peace and of a Dostum spokesman calling for a ceasefire, led to rumours in Kabul on Friday that fighting had stopped.
Taleban fighters on the front line said it had been unusually quiet overnight, but the noise of battle resumed soon after daylight.
